full_judgment:
Mohammad Abdur Rouf J : This appeal, following leave, has been preferred by the heirs of deceased sole plaintiff, Munshi Abdul Khair Faraji of Title Suit No.6 of 1984 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Banaripapa, Bakerganj, from the judgment and order dated 17-8-89 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division (Barisal Bench) in Civil Revision Case No.51 of 1988, discharging the Rule, affirming thereby the order dated 31-1-88 passed by the trial Court refusing the petitioners' prayer for correction and amendment of the plaint of the aforesaid title suit and the decree passed thereon on contest on 27-12-87 by incorporating their names in place of said Munshi Abdul Khair Faraji. 

 2. Late Munshi Abdul Khair Faraji, father of appellant Nos. 1 to 5 and 7 and husband of appellant No.6 instituted Miscellaneous Case No.79(A) of 1984, under Order IX Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, praying for setting aside the ex parte dismissal of the aforesaid suit for default. During pendency of the said Miscellaneous Case, the sole plaintiff-petitioner died on 18-4-85. The appellants on 28-4-85 as the heirs of the said deceased plaintiff, filed an application with a fresh power, seeking permission to proceed with the said Miscellaneous Case as the heirs of the said plaintiff-petitioner. On being allowed they prosecuted the Miscellaneous Case, which was allowed on contest on 27-6-85 and thereby the original suit, TS No.6 of 1984, was restored to its file and number. They also prosecuted the suit, which was ultimately decreed on contest on 27-12-87, declaring the plaintiffs' title to and confirmation of possession in 2.12 acres of land. But the plaint of the suit was not formally amended incorporating the petitioners' names as the substituted heirs of the said deceased plaintiff. Hence the decree was drawn up in the name of the deceased plaintiff. On 30-1-88 the petitioners filed an application under Sections 151,152 and 153 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction and/or amendment of the decree as well as the plaint by incorporating their names in place of the aforesaid deceased plaintiff. The trial Judge by his order dated 31-1-88 rejected the petition on the ground that the same was not maintainable at that stage. The appellant then took a revision, Civil Revision No.51 of 1988, before the High Court Division, Barisal Bench, against the said order of the trial Court and obtained a Rule. It was urged before the High Court Division that due to inadvertence the petitioners' names were not formally incorporated in the plaint in palace of the deceased plaintiff, although they had been allowed as the substituted heirs of the said plaintiff to proceed with the Miscellaneous Case and also with the suit itself. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order discharged the Rule holding, inter alia, that the petitioner’s application dated 28-4-85, filed in the aforementioned Miscellaneous Case, was not an application for substitution but one of seeking permission to conduct the Miscellaneous Case by filing a fresh power. 

 5. Mr Guha further submitted that the appellants application dated 28-4-85, filed before the trial Court in fact and in substance was an application for substitution as well as for acceptance of their power to prosecute the case in place of the deceased plaintiff inasmuch as all the necessary particulars of the legal heirs of the deceased plaintiff for substitution had been furnished before the court for the purpose of getting themselves added as parties in the case and accordingly the application was allowed and they prosecuted the Miscellaneous Case as the substituted heirs of the said plaintiff and thereafter without any objection from the defendants they in the same capacity also prosecuted the suit. At the trial the appellant No.1 as PW 1 deposed for self and others asserting that his father, the original sole plaintiff, had died on 18-4-85 and the trial Court decreed the suit on contest holding, inter alia, that the suit was maintainable (issue No.1) in its the then form and the same was also not bad for defect of parties (issue No.2). The learned Advocate submitted that the trial Court upon acceptance of the said application having allowed the present appellants to prosecute the suit as the substituted heirs of the deceased plaintiff, the learned Judge of the High Court Division upon making out a third case, that the appellants application dated 28-4-85 was not an application for substitution, fell into an error of law in passing the impugned judgment, which is not sustainable in law. 

 8. The learned trial Judge might have been misled, in view of the provision of Order XX rule 3 of the CPC in rejecting the appellants prayer made under section 151, 152 CPC for correction of the plaint of the suit and the decree, presumably on the ground that after the passing of the decree, the court became functus officio to allow amendment of the decree as sought for. The learned Judge of the High Court Division however did not consider that aspect of the, matter, rather he has proceeded on the contents of the application dated 28-4-85 holding that the same was not an application for substitution regarding which we have already expressed our disapproval. 

 9. Now the question is whether non-inclusion of the appellants names as parties to the suit could reasonably be taken by the trial Court as a clerical mistake or an error arising from any accidental slip or omission which should have been corrected by that court, even after passing of the decree in exercise of its authority under section 152 CPC. 

 13. Upon plain reading of the provisions of sub-rule (1) of rule 3 of Order XXII, it appears that it is the right of the heirs of the deceased plaintiff to file is court an application for substitution and a corresponding duty has been cast upon the court to make them parties in the legal proceeding, when the right to sue survives. In exercise of their right the appellants well within the period of limitation submitted the required application for substitution furnishing all the required particulars and the same having been allowed by the court they also prosecuted both the miscellaneous case as well as the suit after this restoration. From the date of acceptance of the appellants' said application there was no legal existence of we deceased plaintiff in the case record, whose name could not have been retained by the trial Court in the plaint when the suit was restored to its file and number, Clearly an error on the face of the record had been committed by the trial Court for not recording the present appellants as substituted plaintiffs in the plaint and refusing to draw up the decree in question accordingly. Under section 152 CPC the trial Court ought to have corrected its own clerical errors even after the passing of the decree. 

 14. Section 152 CPC is based upon the broad principle (i) that any act or omission of the court shall prejudice none of the parties of the proceeding and (ii) that the courts of law by virtue of their very existence as institutions for doing justice shall have a duty to see that their records are true and that they represent correct state of affairs. In that view of the matter the legislative intent under section 152 CPC is that even in the absence of any move by the parties the court of its own motion, in the interest of justice shall make the necessary correction of its record. 

 15. The correction sought for in so far as the impugned decree is concerned is in no way a variation of the decree. This is not unauthorized act under Order XX rule 3 CPC. It is a question of naming the correct plaintiffs in the decree who were allowed to prosecute the suit in place of the deceased plaintiff. Provision of section 152 is like the provision of section 151 CPC. It is a legislative recognition of the court's inherent power to correct its own fault. 

 16. Mr Abdul Aziz sought to argue that no formal application having been made in the suit for making the appellants party to the suit the trial Court had no legal obligation, even under sections 151 and 152 CPC for incorporating their names as substituted plaintiffs in the decree in question by way of correction. This submission of Mr Aziz is not correct and acceptable in view of our above noted finding regarding the court's jurisdiction under the provisions of CPC. 

 For the reasons given above, we allow this appeal without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as the trial Court are set aside and the appellants' application dated 31-1-88 is allowed and accordingly the plaint of the title suit in question and the impugned decree stand corrected by incorporating the appellants name thereof as plaintiffs in place of the deceased sale plaintiff late Munshi Abdul Khair Faraji.
